## The idea

A *canon* gives one melody to two or more voices and delays their entries. The
code is small. The musical constraint is severe: later notes in the subject
must make sense against earlier notes from the same subject.

Entry delay decides which points overlap. Transposition changes the intervals
between voices. Most arbitrary combinations produce exposed seconds, crowded
registers, or cadences that never settle. That failure is the lesson. A subject
for canon carries its accompaniment inside its own sequence.

Begin with equal entries at one-bar distance and no transposition. Then change
one parameter at a time. Keep each voice in an independent thread so the score
data remains shared while timing and register belong to the entry specification.

## Run this

The subject lasts four beats. Three voices enter four beats apart. Each repeats
the subject sixteen times, so the full texture continues for sixteen bars after
the last entry begins.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96

subject = [
  {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 64, start: 0.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 67, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: 65, start: 2.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 64, start: 2.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 62, start: 3.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 60, start: 3.5, duration: 0.5}
]

define :play_events do |events, transpose_by, amp|
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note] + transpose_by,
      release: event[:duration] * 0.8,
      amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

entries = [
  {delay: 0, transpose: 0, synth: :piano, amp: 0.85},
  {delay: 4, transpose: 0, synth: :pluck, amp: 0.65},
  {delay: 8, transpose: -12, synth: :hollow, amp: 0.5}
]

entries.each do |entry|
  in_thread do
    sleep entry[:delay]
    use_synth entry[:synth]
    16.times { play_events subject, entry[:transpose], entry[:amp] }
  end
end
```

The entries are easy to identify because synth and register differ. Once all
three are present, the same contour appears at three points in its cycle.

## Change one thing

1. Change the second delay from 4 to 2. The follower enters halfway through the
   subject. Listen for which note pairs now become exposed. Restore it before
   changing transposition.
2. Set the second transposition to 7. The follower enters a fifth higher. Some
   vertical intervals open, while the register becomes more crowded near the
   first voice.
3. Change the subject's fourth note from 65 to 66. The chromatic pitch meets
   several earlier subject notes. Mark every overlap that sounds unstable rather
   than editing the whole phrase at once.

## Why it works

At a four-beat delay, position one of a follower sounds against position one of
the leader's next repetition. At a two-beat delay, position one sounds against
the middle of the subject. The delay therefore selects a vertical interval map.
You can calculate that map from indexes before rendering.

Consonance alone does not make a good canon. Repeated stable intervals can
sound static, and every voice may reach its cadence at the wrong moment. A
useful subject balances recognisable contour, independent rhythm, and overlap
points that imply changing harmony.

Transposition adds another parameter to the map. A fifth may preserve many
scale relationships but shift the tonal centre. An octave changes register
without changing pitch class. Test delay first, then transposition, so the cause
of a bad overlap stays visible.

The shared subject array is immutable score data. Entry records contain delay,
transposition, synth, and amplitude. This is the same separation used for form
and rendering: one musical object, several calls with different arguments.

The absolute `:start` values keep the subject compatible with `play_events`
from the transcription and capstone chapters. Repetition resets the renderer's
cursor at the start of each four-beat subject. Entry delay remains outside the
subject because it belongs to the voice that imitates, not to the melody being
imitated.

## Take it further

Write an eight-beat subject and build a three-voice canon that lasts at least
sixteen bars. Test entry delays of two, four, and eight beats, then choose one.
Test unison, octave, and fifth transpositions separately. The target is a
version with no edit to the subject between voices, independently inspectable
entry data, and comments naming the three most exposed overlaps and the implied
chords at those moments.
